entries.30cc399445fe2174130a9f71b6392997c039a62d: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen23748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23749" type="x-p"/> The wise - The person who follows the dictates of wisdom, as mentioned above, shall inherit glory; because, being one of the heavenly family, a child of God, he has thereby heaven for his inheritance; but fools, such as those mentioned chapters 1 and 2, shall have ignominy for their exaltation. Many such fools as Solomon speaks of are exalted to the gibbet and gallows. The way to prevent this and the like evils, is to attend to the voice of wisdom. <div eID="gen23749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23750" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23751" type="x-p"/> My son - The preceptor continues to deliver his lessons. <div eID="gen23751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23752" type="x-p"/> Forget not my law - Remember what thou hast heard, and practice what thou dost remember; and let all obedience be from the heart: "Let thy heart keep my commandments."

entries.875959bf115fc795ed102b1b2257e8630f611c1d: <div eID="gen10603" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">FOURTH INTRODUCTORY MASHAL DISCOURSE, III. 1-18.</title> <title type="x-s3">EXHORTATION TO LOVE AND FAITHFULNESS, AND SELF-SACRIFICING DEVOTION TO GOD, AS THE TRUE WISDOM.</title> <div sID="gen10604" type="x-p"/> The foregoing Mashal discourse seeks to guard youth against ruinous companionship ; this points out to them more particularly the relation toward God and man, which alone can make them truly happy, vers. 1-4. <div eID="gen10604" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen10605"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10606"/>1 My son, forget not my doctrine,<l eID="gen10606" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10607"/>And let thine heart keep my commandments ;<l eID="gen10607" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10608"/>2 For length of days, and years of life,<l eID="gen10608" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10609"/>And peace, -will they add to thee.<l eID="gen10609" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10610"/>3 Let not kindness and truth forsake thee :<l eID="gen10610" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10611"/>Bind them about thy neck,<l eID="gen10611" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10612"/>Write them on the tablet of thy heart,<l eID="gen10612" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10613"/>4 And obtain favour and true prudence<l eID="gen10613" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10614"/>In the eyes of God and of men.<l eID="gen10614" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen10605"/> <div sID="gen10615" type="x-p"/> The admonition takes a new departure, תּוֹרָתִ֣י and וּ֝מִצְוֺתַ֗י refer to the following new discourse and laws of conduct. Here, in the midst of the discourse, we have יִצֹּ֥ר and not יִגְצֹּ֥ר ; the non-assimilated form is found only in the conclusion, e.g. ii. 11, v. 2. The plur. יוֹסִ֥יפוּ (ver. 2) for חּוֹטֵפְנָח (they will bring, add) refers to the doctrine and the precepts ; the synallage has its ground in this, that the fem. construction in Hebrew is not applicable in such a case ; the vulgar Arab, also has set aside the forms jaktubna, taktubna. “Extension of days” is continuance of duration, stretching itself out according to the promise, Ex. 20:12; and “years of life” (9:11) are years — namely, many of them — of a life which is life in the full sense of the word. חַיִּ֑ים has here the pregnant signification vita vitalis, βίος βιωτός (Fl.). שָׁל֗וֹם (R. של) is pure well-being, free from all that disturbs peace or satisfaction, internal and external contentment.
entries.b18dc2f64314b4086208a858e497a706f22cd214: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference> <div eID="gen10615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10616" type="x-p"/> With this verse the doctrine begins; אל (not לא) shows the 3a does not continue the promise of Pro 3:2. חסד (R. חם, <hi type="italic">stringere, afficere</hi>) is, according to the prevailing usage of the language, well-affectedness, it may be of God toward men, or of men toward God, or of men toward one another - a loving disposition, of the same meaning as the N.T. ἀγάπη (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Hos 6:6). אמת (from אמנת), continuance, a standing to one’s promises, and not falsifying just expectations; thus fidelity, πίστις, in the interrelated sense of <hi type="italic">fides</hi> and <hi type="italic">fidelitas</hi>. These two states of mind and of conduct are here contemplated as moral powers (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.8">Psa 61:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.43.3">Psa 43:3</reference>), which are of excellent service, and bring precious gain; and 4b shows that their ramification on the side of God and of men, the religious and the moral, remains radically inseparable. The suffix  ם does not refer to the doctrine and the precepts, but to these two cardinal virtues. If the disciple is admonished to bind them about his neck (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Pro 1:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.22">Pro 3:22</reference>), so here reference is made, not to ornament, nor yet to protection against evil influences by means of them, as by an amulet<note placement="foot">Fleischer is here reminded of the giraffe in the Jardin des Plantes, the head of which was adorned by its Arabic keeper with strings and jewels, the object of which was to turn aside the ‛ain [the bad, mischievous look] from the precious beast.</note> (for which proofs are wanting), but to the signet which was wont to be constantly carried (<reference osisRef="Gen.38.18">Gen 38:18</reference>, cf. Sol 8:6) on a string around the neck. The parallel member 3c confirms this; 3b and 3c together put us in mind of the <hi type="italic">Tephillim</hi> (phylacteries), <reference osisRef="Exod.13.16">Exo 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.8">Deu 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.18">Deu 11:18</reference>, in which what is here a figure is presented in external form, but as the real figure of that which is required in the inward parts. לוּח (from לוּח, Arab. l'ah, to begin to shine, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, of a shooting star, gleaming sword; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Wetzstein, <hi type="italic">Deutsch. morgenl. Zeitschr</hi>. xxii. 151f.) signifies the tablet prepared for writing by means of polish; to write love and fidelity on the tablet of the heart, is to impress deeply on the heart the duty of both virtues, so that one will be impelled to them from within outward (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.33">Jer 31:33</reference>).
entries.795e5910459a0469b15228891da818bca161d38f: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">Pro 3:4</reference> <div eID="gen10616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10617" type="x-p"/> To the admonitory imper. there follows here a second, as <reference osisRef="Prov.4.4">Pro 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.13">Pro 20:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.4">Amo 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.20">2Ch 20:20</reference>, instead of which also the perf. consec. might stand; the counsellor wishes, with the good to which he advises, at the same time to present its good results. שׂכל is (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.3">1Sa 25:3</reference>) the appearance, for the Arab. shakl means <hi type="italic">forma</hi>, as uniting or binding the lineaments or contours into one figure, σχῆμα, according to which שׂכל טוב may be interpreted of the pleasing and advantageous impression which the well-built external appearance of a man makes, as an image of that which his internal excellence produces; thus, favourable view, friendly judgment, good reputation (Ewald, Hitzig, Zöckler). But everywhere else (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.15">Pro 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.22">2Ch 30:22</reference>) this phrase means good, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, fine, well-becoming insight, or prudence; and שׂכל has in the language of the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi> no other meaning than <hi type="italic">intellectus</hi>, which proceeds from the inwardly forming activity of the mind. He obtains favour in the eyes of God and man, to whom favour on both sides is shown; he obtains refined prudence, to whom it is on both sides adjudicated. It is unnecessary, with Ewald and Hitzig, to assign the two objects to God and men. In the eyes of both at the same time, he who carries love and faithfulness in his heart appears as one to whom חן and שׂכל טוב must be adjudicated.
entries.af7812e0b9e79d2afa19023dfcbe3b3b4732c370: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.5-Prov.3.8">Pro 3:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen10617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10618" type="x-p"/> Were “kindness and truth” (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference>) understood only in relation to men, then the following admonition would not be interposed, since it proceeds from that going before, if there the quality of kindness and truth, not only towards man, but also towards God, is commended: 5 Trust in Jahve with thy whole heart,    And lean not on thine own understanding. 6 In all thy ways acknowledge Him,    And He will make plain thy paths. 7 Be not wise in thine own eyes;    Fear Jahve, and depart from evil. 8 Health will then come to thy navel,    And refreshing to thy bones. <div eID="gen10618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10619" type="x-p"/> From God alone comes true prosperity, true help. He knows the right way to the right ends. He knows what benefits us. He is able to free us from that which does us harm: therefore it is our duty and our safety to place our confidence wholly in Him, and to trust not to our own judgment. The verb בּטח, Arab. baṭḥ, has the root-meaning <hi type="italic">expandere</hi>, whence perhaps, by a more direct way than that noted under <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>, it acquires the meaning <hi type="italic">confidere</hi>, to lean with the whole body on something, in order to rest upon it, strengthened by על, if one lean wholly - Fr. <hi type="italic">se reposer sur quelqu'un</hi>; Ital. <hi type="italic">riposarsi sopra alcuno</hi>, - like השּׁען with אל, to lean on anything, so as to be supported by it; with על, to support oneself on anything (Fl.). דעהוּ (the same in form as שׂאהוּ, Num 11:12) is not fully represented by “acknowledge Him;” as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.9">1Ch 28:9</reference> it is not a mere theoretic acknowledgment that is meant, but earnest penetrating cognizance, engaging the whole man. The practico-mystical דעהוּ, in and of itself full of significance, according to O. and N.T. usage, is yet strengthened by <hi type="italic">toto corde</hi>. The heart is the central seat of all spiritual soul-strength; to love God with the whole heart is to concentrate the whole inner life on the active contemplation of God, and the ready observance of His will. God requites such as show regard to Him, by making plain their path before them, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, by leading them directly to the right end, removing all hindrances out of their way. ארחתיך has <hi type="italic">Cholem</hi> in the first syllable (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kimchi’s <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.).<note placement="foot">In the st. constr. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.19">Pro 2:19</reference>, and with the grave suff. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>, ǒ instead of ō is in order; but Ben-Asher’s ארחתי, <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.33.11">Job 33:11</reference>, is an inconsistency.</note> “Be not wise in thine own eyes” is equivalent to <hi type="italic">ne tibi sapiens videare</hi>; for, as J. H. Michaelis remarks, <hi type="italic">confidere Deo est sapere, sibi vero ac suae sapientiae, desipere</hi>. “Fear God and depart from evil” is the twofold representation of the εὐσέβεια, or practical piety, in the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> writings: <reference osisRef="Prov.16.6">Pro 16:6</reference>, the Mashal <reference osisRef="Ps.34.10">Psa 34:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.15">Psa 34:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference> cf. Pro 1:2. For סר מרע, the post-biblical expression is ירא חטא.
entries.9f68190a87003c437f401aeb6a287c27f6ce133a: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.9-Prov.3.10">Pro 3:9-10</reference>  Honour Jahve with thy wealth,    And with the first-fruits of all thine increase: 10 Then shall thy barns be filled with plenty,    And thy vats overflow with must. <div eID="gen10620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10621" type="x-p"/> It may surprise us that the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, being separated from the ceremonial law, here commends the giving of tithes. But in the first place, the consciousness of the duty of giving tithes is older than the Mosaic law, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.22">Gen 28:22</reference>; in this case, the giving of tithes is here a general ethical expression. עשּׂר and מעשׂר do not occur in the Book of Proverbs; in the post-biblical phraseology the tithes are called חלק הגּבהּ, the portion of the Most High. כּבּד, as the Arab. waḳḳra, to make heavy, then to regard and deal with as weighty and solemn (opp. קלּל, to regard and treat as light, from קלל = Arab. hân, to be light). הון, properly lightness in the sense of <hi type="italic">aisance</hi>, opulency, forms with כּבּד an oxymoron (<hi type="italic">fac Jovam gravem de levitate tua</hi>), but one aimed at by the author neither at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.13">Pro 1:13</reference> nor here. מן (in מהונך and 'מר, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.9">Pro 3:9</reference>) is in both cases partitive, as in the law of the Levitical tenths, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.30">Lev 27:30</reference>, and of the <hi type="italic">Challa</hi> (heave-offering of dough), Num 15:21, where also ראשׁית (in <reference osisRef="Heb.7.4">Heb 7:4</reference>, ἀκροθίνια) occurs in a similar sense, cf. Num 18:12 (in the law of the <hi type="italic">Theruma</hi> or wave-offering of the priests), as also תּבוּאה in the law of the second tenths, <reference osisRef="Deut.14.22">Deu 14:22</reference>, cf. Num 18:30 (in the law of the tenths of the priests).
entries.ce1d82cca7c2fe649942aa24ee16b6926d4c10cd: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.11-Prov.3.12">Pro 3:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen10622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10623" type="x-p"/> The contrast here follows. As God should not be forgotten in days of prosperity, so one should not suffer himself to be estranged from Him by days of adversity. 11 The school of Jahve, my son, despise thou not,      Nor loathe thou His correction; 12 For Jahve correcteth him whom He loveth,      And that as a father his son whom he loveth<hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., the original passage Job 5:17. There is not for the Book of Job a more suitable motto than this tetrastich, which expresses its fundamental thought, that there is a being chastened and tried by suffering which has as its motive the love of God, and which does not exclude sonship.<note placement="foot">Here Procop. rightly distinguishes between παιδεία and τιμωρία.</note> <div eID="gen10623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10624" type="x-p"/> One may say that <reference osisRef="Prov.3.11">Pro 3:11</reference> expresses the problem of the Book of Job, and <reference osisRef="Prov.3.12">Pro 3:12</reference> its solution. מוּסר, παιδεία, we have translated “school,” for יסּר, παιδεύειν, means in reality to take one into school. <hi type="italic">Ahndung</hi> [punishment] or <hi type="italic">Rüge</hi> [reproof] is the German word which most corresponds to the Hebr. תּוכחה or תּוכחת. קוּץ ב (whence here the prohibitive תּקץ with אל) means to experience loathing (disgust) at anything, or aversion (vexation) toward anything. The lxx (cited Heb 12:5.), μηδὲ ἐκλύου, nor be faint-hearted, which joins in to the general thought, that we should not be frightened away from God, or let ourselves be estranged from Him by the attitude of anger in which He appears in His determination to inflict suffering. In 12a the accentuation leaves it undefined whether יהוה as subject belongs to the relative or to the principal clause; the traditional succession of accents, certified also by Ben Bileam, is כי את אשׁר יאהב יהוה, for this passage belongs to the few in which more than three servants (viz., <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>, <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>, and three <hi type="italic">Munachs</hi>) go before the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 19; <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, vi. §6; the differences between Ben-Asher and Ben-Naphtali in the Appendixes to <hi type="italic">Biblia Rabbinica</hi>; Dachselt’s <hi type="italic">Biblia Accentuata</hi>, and Pinner’s <hi type="italic">Prospectus</hi>, p. 91 (Odessa, 1845).</note> <div eID="gen10624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10625" type="x-p"/> The further peculiarity is here to be observed, that את, although without the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, retains its <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>, besides here only in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference>; Psa 60:2. 12b is to be interpreted thus (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">Pro 9:5</reference>): “and (that) as a father the son, whom he loves.” The ו is explanatory, as <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.3">1Sa 28:3</reference> (Gesenius, §155, 1a), and ירצה (which one may supplement by אתו or בּו) is a defining clause having the force of a clause with אשׁר. The translation <hi type="italic">et ut pater qui filio bene cupit</hi>, is syntactically (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa 40:11</reference>) and accentually (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., 13b) not less admissible, but translating “and as a father he holds his son dear,” or with Hitzig (after <reference osisRef="Jer.31.10">Jer 31:10</reference>, a passage not quite syntactically the same), “and holds him dear, as a father his son” (which Zöckler without syntactical authority prefers on account of the 2nd modus, cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.18">Psa 51:18</reference>), does not seem a right parallel clause, since the giving of correction is the chief point, and the love only the accompanying consideration (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.24">Pro 13:24</reference>). According to our interpretation, יוכיח is to be carried forward in the mind from 12a. The lxx find the parallel word in יכאב, for they translate μαστιγοῖ δὲ πάντα υἱὸν, ὃν παραδέχεται, and thus have read יכאב or ויכאב.
entries.3906892d49224ca63bcd7c80e9120587fe936849: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.13-Prov.3.14">Pro 3:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen10625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10626" type="x-p"/> Such submission to God, the All-wise, the All-directing, who loves us with fatherly affection, is wisdom, and such wisdom is above all treasures. 13 Blessed is the man who has found wisdom,      And the man who has gained understanding; 14 For better is her acquisition than the acquisition of silver,      And her gain than fine gold. 15 More precious is she than corals;      And all thy jewels do not equal her value. <div eID="gen10626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10627" type="x-p"/> The imperfect יפיק, which as the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of פּוּק, <hi type="italic">exire</hi>, has the general meaning <hi type="italic">educere</hi>, interchanges with the perfect מצא. This bringing forth is either a delivering up, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, giving out or presenting, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">Isa 58:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.140.9">Psa 140:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.13">Psa 144:13</reference> (cf. נפק, Arab. nafaḳ, to give out, to pay out), or a fetching out, getting out, receiving, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.35">Pro 8:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference>; Pro 18:22. Thus 13a reminds one of the parable of the treasure in the field, and 13b of that of the goodly pearl for which the ἔμπορος who sought the pearl parted with all that he had. Here also is declared the promise of him who trades with a merchant for the possession of wisdom; for סחרהּ and סחר (both, as <reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">Isa 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa 45:15</reference>, from סחר, the latter after the forms זרע, נטע, without our needing to assume a second primary form, סחר) go back to the root-word סחר, to trade, go about as a trader, with the fundamental meaning ἐμπορεύεσθαι (lxx); and also the mention of the pearls is not wanting here, for at all events the meaning “pearls” has blended itself with פּנינים, which is a favourite word in the Mashal poetry, though it be not the original meaning of the word. In 14b כּסף is surpassed by חרוּץ (besides in the Proverbs, found only in this meaning in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.14">Psa 68:14</reference>), which properly means ore found in a mine, from חרץ, to cut in, to dig up, and hence the poetic name of gold, perhaps of gold dug out as distinguished from molten gold. Hitzig regards χρυσός as identical with it; but this word (Sanskr. without the ending hir, Zench. zar) is derived from ghar, to glitter (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Curtius). תּבוּאתהּ we have translated “gain,” for it does not mean the profit which wisdom brings, the tribute which it yields, but the gain, the possession of wisdom herself.
entries.4e00c2de91437dca986163d8d2de7187d02cb4ab: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.15">Pro 3:15</reference> <div eID="gen10627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10628" type="x-p"/> As regards פּנינים, for which the <hi type="italic">Kethîb</hi> has פּניּים, the following things are in favour of the fundamental meaning “corals,” viz.: (1.) The name itself, which corresponds with the Arab. fann; this word, proceeding from the root-idea of shooting forth, particularly after the manner of plants, means the branch and all that raises or multiplies itself branch-like or twig-like (Fleischer). (2.) The redness attributed to the פנינים, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.7">Lam 4:7</reference>, in contradistinction to the pure whiteness attributed to snow and milk (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Job.28.18">Job 28:18</reference>). The meaning of the word may, however, have become generalized in practice (lxx <hi type="italic">in loc</hi>. λίθων πολετελῶν, <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> λιθιδίων); the meaning “pearls,” given to it in the Job-Targum by Rashi, and particularly by Bochart, lay so much the nearer as one may have wrought also corals and precious stones, such as the carbuncle, sardius, and sapphire, into the form of pearls. יקרה, in consequence of the retrogression of the tone, has <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., and that as an exception, as has been remarked by the Masora, since in substantives and proper names terminating in  ה the נסוג אחור, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the receding of the tone, does not elsewhere appear, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, יפה היא, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.14">Gen 12:14</reference>, בּרה היא, Sol 6:9, צרה היא, Jer 30:7. חפץ is first <hi type="italic">abstr</hi>., a being inclined to something, lust, will, pleasure in anything, then also <hi type="italic">concr</hi>., anything in which one has pleasure, what is beautiful, precious; cf. Arab. nfı̂s,  hyy, hence hjârt nfı̂st, precious stones” (Fleischer). שׁוה with ב means to be an equivalent (purchase-price, exchange) for anything; the most natural construction in Arab. as well as in Hebr. is that with ל, to be the equivalent of a thing (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job 33:27</reference>); the ב is the <hi type="italic">Beth pretii</hi>, as if one said in Arab.: biabi anta thou art in the estimate of my father, I give it for thee. One distinctly perceives in <reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">Pro 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.15">Pro 3:15</reference>, the echo of Job 28. This tetrastich occurs again with a slight variation at <reference osisRef="Prov.8.10">Pro 8:10</reference>-11. The Talmud and the Midrash accent it so, that in the former the expression is וכל־חפצים, and in the latter וכל־חפציך, and they explain the latter of precious stones and pearls (אבנים טובות ומרגליות).
entries.f21b88f75e7f525f02b1125761dd88a473960acf: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.16-Prov.3.18">Pro 3:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen10628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10629" type="x-p"/> That wisdom is of such incomparable value is here confirmed: 16 Length of days is in her right hand;      In her left, riches and honour. 17 Her ways are pleasant ways,      And all her paths are peace. 18 A tree of life is she to those that lay hold upon her,      And he who always holdeth her fast is blessed. <div eID="gen10629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10630" type="x-p"/> As in the right hand of Jahve, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>, are pleasures for evermore, so Wisdom holds in her right hand “length of days,” viz., of the days of life, thus life, the blessing of blessings; in her left, riches and honour (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.18">Pro 8:18</reference>), the two good things which, it is true, do not condition life, but, received from Wisdom, and thus wisely, elevate the happiness of life-in the right hand is the chief good, in the left the προσθήκη, Mat 6:33. Didymus: <hi type="italic">Per sapientiae dextram divinarum rerum cognitio, ex qua immortalitatis vita oritur, significatur; per sinistram autem rerum humanarum notitia, ex qua gloria opumque abundantia nascitur</hi>. The lxx, as between 15a and 15b, so also here after <reference osisRef="Prov.3.16">Pro 3:16</reference>, interpolate two lines: “From her mouth proceedeth righteousness; justice and mercy she bears upon her tongue,” - perhaps translated from the Hebr., but certainly added by a reader.
entries.8a76f417c1743d1b5854325e26a726684431a560: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.19-Prov.3.20">Pro 3:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen10630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10631" type="x-p"/> This place of a mediatrix - the speaker here now continues - she had from the beginning. God’s world-creating work was mediated by her: 19 Jahve hath by wisdom founded the earth,      Established the heavens by understanding. 20 By His knowledge the water-floods broke forth,      And the sky dropped down dew. <div eID="gen10631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10632" type="x-p"/> That wisdom is meant by which God planned the world-idea, and now also wrought it out; the wisdom in which God conceived the world ere it was framed, and by which also He gave external realization to His thoughts; the wisdom which is indeed an attribute of God and a characteristic of His actions, since she is a property of His nature, and His nature attests itself in her, but not less, as appears, not from this group of tetrastichs, but from all that has hitherto been said, and form the personal testimony, Pro 8:22., of which it is the <hi type="italic">praeludium</hi>, she goes forth as a divine power to which God has given to have life in herself. Considered apart from the connection of these discourses, this group of verses, as little as <reference osisRef="Jer.10.2">Jer 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.24">Psa 104:24</reference>, determines regarding the attributive interpretation; the Jerusalem Targum, I, when it translates, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1">Gen 1:1</reference>, בראשׁית by בּחוּכמא (בּחוּכמתא), combines <reference osisRef="Prov.8.22">Pro 8:22</reference> with such passages as this before us. יסד (here with the tone thrown back) properly signifies, like the Arab. wasad, to lay fast, to found, for one gives to a fact the firm basis of its existence. The parallel <hi type="italic">Pil</hi>. of כּוּן (Arab. kân, cogn. כהן, see on Isaiah, p. 691) signifies to set up, to restore; here equivalent to, to give existence.
entries.5b5d2c1f93561f63ee32778306ccd1776b7a107e: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.21-Prov.3.22">Pro 3:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen10633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10634" type="x-p"/> From this eminence, in which the work of creation presents wisdom, exhortations are now deduced, since the writer always expresses himself only with an ethical intention regarding the nature of wisdom: 21 My son, may they not depart from thine eyes -      Preserve thoughtfulness and consideration, 22 And they will be life to thy soul      And grace to thy neck. <div eID="gen10634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10635" type="x-p"/> If we make the synonyms of wisdom which are in 21b the subject <hi type="italic">per prolepsin</hi> to אל־ילזוּ (Hitzig and Zöckler), then <reference osisRef="Prov.3.19-Prov.3.20">Pro 3:19-20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.3.21-Prov.3.22">Pro 3:21-22</reference> clash. The subjects are wisdom, understanding, knowledge, which belong to God, and shall from His become the possession of those who make them their aim. Regarding לוּז, <hi type="italic">obliquari, deflectere</hi>, see under <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.21">Pro 4:21</reference>; regarding תּשׁיּה (here <hi type="italic">defective</hi> after the Masora, as rightly in Vened. 1515, 1521, and Nissel, 1662), see at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>; ילזוּ for תּלזנה, see at Pro 3:2. The lxx (cf. <reference osisRef="Heb.2.1">Heb 2:1</reference>) translate without distinctness of reference: υἱὲ μὴ παραῤῥυῂς (παραρυῇς), let it now flow past, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, let it not be unobserved, hold it always before thee; the Targ. with the Syr. render לא נזּל, <hi type="italic">ne vilescat</hi>, as if the words were אל־יזוּלוּ. In 22a the <hi type="italic">synallage generis</hi> is continued: ויהיוּ for ותהיינה. Regarding גּרגּרת, see at Pro 1:9. By wisdom the soul gains life, divinely true and blessed, and the external appearance of the man grace, which makes him pleasing and gains for him affection.
entries.57c3c231f8832afd2bc8907996600e1bc572ebb6: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.23-Prov.3.26">Pro 3:23-26</reference> <div eID="gen10635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10636" type="x-p"/> But more than this, wisdom makes its possessor in all situations of life confident in God: 23 Then shalt thou go thy way with confidence,      And thy foot shall not stumble. 24 When thou liest down, thou are not afraid,      But thou layest thyself down and hast sweet sleep. 25 Thou needest not be afraid of sudden alarm,      Nor for the storm of the wicked when it breaketh forth. 26 For Jahve will be thy confidence      And keep thy foot from the snare. <div eID="gen10636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10637" type="x-p"/> The לבטח (cf. our “<hi type="italic">bei guter Laune</hi>” = in good cheer), with ל of the condition, is of the same meaning as the conditional adverbial accusative בּטח, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.9">Pro 10:9</reference>; Pro 1:33. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.23">Pro 3:23</reference> the lxx translate ὁ δὲ πούς σου οὐ μὴ προσκόψῃ, while, on the contrary, at <reference osisRef="Ps.91.12">Psa 91:12</reference> they make the person the subject (μήποτε προσκόψῃς τὸν κ.τ.λ.); here also we retain more surely the subject from 23a, especially since for the intrans. of נגף (to smite, to push) a <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. התנגּף is used Jer 13:16. In <reference osisRef="Prov.3.24">Pro 3:24</reference> there is the echo of <reference osisRef="Job.11.18">Job 11:18</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Prov.3.25">Pro 3:25</reference> of Job 5:21. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.24">Pro 3:24</reference> is altogether the same as <reference osisRef="Job.5.24">Job 5:24</reference> : <hi type="italic">et decumbes et suavis erit somnus tuus = si decubueris, suavis erit</hi>. The hypothetic perf., according to the sense, is both there and at <reference osisRef="Job.11.18">Job 11:18</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jer 20:9</reference>) oxytoned as <hi type="italic">perf. consec.</hi> Similar examples are <reference osisRef="Prov.6.22">Pro 6:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.33.13">Gen 33:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.31">1Sa 25:31</reference>, cf. Ewald, §357a. ערבה (of sleep as <reference osisRef="Jer.31.26">Jer 31:26</reference>) is from ערב, which in Hebr. is used of pleasing impressions, as the Arab. ‛ariba of a lively, free disposition. שׁנה, <hi type="italic">somnus</hi> (<hi type="italic">nom. actionis</hi> from ישׁן, with the ground-form sina preserved in the Arab. lidat, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Job, p. 284, note), agrees in inflexion with שׁנה, <hi type="italic">annus</hi>. אל, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.25">Pro 3:25</reference>, denies, like <reference osisRef="Ps.121.3">Psa 121:3</reference>, with emphasis: be afraid only not = thou hast altogether nothing to fear. Schultens rightly says: <hi type="italic">Subest species prohibitionis et tanquam abominationis, ne tale quicquam vel in suspicionem veniat in mentemve cogitando admittatur</hi>. פּחד here means terror, as Pro 1:26., the terrific object; פּתאם (with the accus. om) is the virtual genitive, as <reference osisRef="Prov.26.2">Pro 26:2</reference> חנּם (with accus. am). Regarding שׁאה, see under Pro 1:27. The genitive רשׁעים may be, after <reference osisRef="Ps.37.18">Psa 37:18</reference>, the <hi type="italic">genit. subjecti</hi>, but still it lies nearer to say that he who chooses the wisdom of God as his guiding star has no ground to fear punishment as transgressors have reason to fear it; the שׁאה is meant which wisdom threatens against transgressors, Pro 1:27. He needs have no fear of it, for wisdom is a gift of God, and binds him who receives it to the giver: Jahve becomes and is henceforth his confidence. Regarding ב <hi type="italic">essentiae</hi>, which expresses the closest connection of the subject with the predicate which it introduces, see under Psa 35:2. As here, so also at <reference osisRef="Exod.18.4">Exo 18:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">Psa 118:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.146.6">Psa 146:6</reference>, the predicate is a noun with a pronominal suffix. כּסל is, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.78.7">Psa 78:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.24">Job 31:24</reference>, cognate to מבטה and מקוה,<note placement="foot">According to Malbim, תּקוה is the expectation of good, and כּסל, confidence in the presence of evil.</note> the object and ground of confidence. That the word in other connections may mean also fool-hardiness, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference>, and folly, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.25">Ecc 7:25</reference> (cf. regarding כּסיל, which in Arab. as belı̂d denotes the dull, in Hebr. fools, see under <reference osisRef="Prov.1.22">Pro 1:22</reference>), it follows that it proceeds from the fundamental conception of fulness of flesh and of fat, whence arise the conceptions of dulness and slothfulness, as well as of confidence, whether confidence in self or in God (see Schultens <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, and Wünsche’s <hi type="italic">Hosea</hi>, p. 207f.). לכד is taking, catching, as in a net or trap or pit, from לכד, to catch (cf. Arab. lakida, to fasten, III, IV to hold fast); another root-meaning, in which Arab. lak connects itself with nak, nk, to strike, to assail (whence al-lakdat, the assault against the enemy, Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitsch. xxii. 140), is foreign to the Hebr. Regarding the מן of מלכד, Fleischer remarks: “The מן after the verbs of guarding, preserving, like שׁמר and נצר, properly expresses that one by those means holds or seeks to hold a person or thing back from something, like the Lat. <hi type="italic">defendere, tueri aliquem ab hostibus, a perculo</hi>.”<note placement="foot">Hitzig rejects <reference osisRef="Prov.3.22-Prov.3.26">Pro 3:22-26</reference> as a later interpolation. And why? Because chap. 3, which he regards as a complete discourse, consists of twice ten verses beginning with בּני. In addition to this symmetry other reasons easily reveal themselves to his penetration. But the discourses contained in chap. 1-9 do not all begin with בני (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pro 1:20</reference>); and when it stands in the beginning of the discourse, it is not always the first word (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>); and when it occurs as the first word or in the first line, it does not always commence a new discourse (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.15">Pro 1:15</reference> in the middle of the first, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.11">Pro 3:11</reference> in the middle of the fourth); and, moreover, the Hebr. poetry and oratory does not reckon according to verses terminated by <hi type="italic">Soph Pasuk</hi>, which are always accented distichs, but they in reality frequently consist of three or more lines. The rejected verses are in nothing unlike those that remain, and which are undisputed; they show the same structure of stichs, consisting for the most part of three, but sometimes also only of two words (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.22">Pro 3:22</reference> with <reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Pro 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.10">Pro 1:10</reference>), the same breadth in the course of the thoughts, and the same accord with Job and Deuteronomy.</note>
entries.e7837c832cbc2e72c07e0a3a3084bc18e76f6f9f: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.27-Prov.3.28">Pro 3:27-28</reference> <div eID="gen10637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10638" type="x-p"/> The first illustration of neighbourly love which is recommended, is readiness to serve: 27 Refuse no manner of good to him to whom it is due      When it is in thy power to do it. 28 Say not to thy neighbour, “Go, and come again,      To-morrow I will give it,” whilst yet thou hast it. <div eID="gen10638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10639" type="x-p"/> Regarding the intensive plur. בּעליו with a sing. meaning, see under Pro 1:19. The form of expression without the suffix is not בּעלי but בּעל טוב; and this denotes here, not him who does good (בעל as Arab. dhw or ṣaḥab), but him to whom the good deed is done (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">Pro 17:8</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as here, him who is worthy of it (בעל as Arab. âhl), him who is the man for it (Jewish interp.: מי שׁהוא ראוי לו). We must refuse nothing good (nothing either legally or morally good) to him who has a right to it (מנע מן as <reference osisRef="Job.22.7">Job 22:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.16">Job 31:16</reference>),<note placement="foot">Accentuate אל־תמנע טוב, not אל־תמנע־טוב. The doubling of the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> is purposeless, and, on the contrary, the separating of טוב from מבעליו by the Dechi (the separating accent subordinate to <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>) is proper. It is thus in the best MSS.</note> if we are in a condition to do him this good. The phrase ישׁ־לאל ידי, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.29">Gen 31:29</reference>, and frequently, signifies: it is belonging to (practicable) the power of my hand, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, I have the power and the means of doing it. As זד signifies the haughty, insolent, but may be also used in the neuter of insolent conduct (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Psa 19:14</reference>), so אל signifies the strong, but also (although only in this phrase) strength. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> rejects the plur. ידיך, because elsewhere the hand always follows לאל in the singular. But it rejects the plur. לרעיך (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.28">Pro 3:28</reference>) because the address following is directed to one person. Neither of these emendations was necessary. The usage of the language permits exceptions, notwithstanding the <hi type="italic">usus tyrannus</hi>, and the plur. לרעיך may be interpreted distributively: to thy fellows, it may be this one or that one. Hitzig also regards לרעיך as a singular; but the masc. of רעיה, the ground-form of which is certainly ra‛j, is רעה, or shorter, רע. לך ושׁוּב does not mean: forth! go home again! but: go, and come again. שׁוּב, to come again, to return to something, to seek it once more.<note placement="foot">Thus also (Arab.) raj' is used in Thaalebi’s <hi type="italic">Confidential Companion</hi>, p. 24, line 3, of Flügel’s ed. Admission was prevented to one Haschmid, then angry he sought it once more; he was again rejected, then he sought it not again (Arab. flm yraj'), but says, etc. Flügel has misunderstood the passage. Fleischer explains raj', with reference to <reference osisRef="Prov.3.28">Pro 3:28</reference>, by <hi type="italic">revenir à la charge</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen10639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10640" type="x-p"/> The ו of ישׁו אתּך is, as 29b, the conditional: <hi type="italic">quum sit penes te, sc. quod ei des</hi>. “To-morrow shall I give” is less a promise than a delay and putting off, because it is difficult for him to alienate himself from him who makes the request. This holding fast by one’s own is unamiable selfishness; this putting off in the fulfilment of one’s duty is a sin of omission - οὐ γὰρ οἶδας, as the lxx adds, τὶ τέξεται ἡ ἐπιοῦσα.
entries.e04f704eaed5a6a259f4a910e7efca68ff053fc9: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.29">Pro 3:29</reference> <div eID="gen10640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10641" type="x-p"/> A second illustration of neighbourly love is harmlessness: <div eID="gen10641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10642" type="x-p"/> Devise not evil against thy neighbour, <div eID="gen10642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10643" type="x-p"/> While he dwelleth securely by thee. <div eID="gen10643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10644" type="x-p"/> The verb חרשׁ, χαράσσειν, signifies to cut into, and is used of the <hi type="italic">faber ferrarius</hi> as well as of the τιγναριυς (Isaiah, p. 463), who with a cutting instrument (חרשׁ, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.22">Gen 4:22</reference>) works with metal or wood, and from his profession is called חרשׁ. But the word means as commonly to plough, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to cut with the plough, and חרשׁ is used also of a ploughman, and, without any addition to it, it always has this meaning. It is then a question whether the metaphorical phrase רעה חרשׁ signifies to fabricate evil, cf. <hi type="italic">dolorum faber, mendacia procudere</hi>, ψευδῶν καὶ ἀπατῶν τέκτων, and the Homeric κακὰ φρεὶ βυσσοδομεύειν (Fleischer and most others), or to plough evil (Rashi, Ewald, etc.). The Targ., Syriac, and Jerome translate חשׁב, without deciding the point, by <hi type="italic">moliri</hi>; but the lxx and <hi type="italic">Graecus Venet</hi>. by τεκταίνειν. The correctness of these renderings is not supported by Ezek. 21:36, where חרשׁי משׁחית are not such as fabricate destruction, but smiths who cause destruction; also מחרישׁ, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">1Sa 23:9</reference>, proves nothing, and probably does not at all appertain to חרשׁ <hi type="italic">incidere</hi> (Keil), but to חרשׁ <hi type="italic">silere</hi>, in the sense of <hi type="italic">dolose moliri</hi>. On the one hand, it is to be observed from <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>; Hos 10:13, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>, that the meaning <hi type="italic">arare malum</hi> might connect itself with חרשׁ רעה; and the proverb of Sirach 7:12, μὴ ἀροτρία ψεῦδος ἐπ ̓ ἀδελφῷ σου, places this beyond a doubt. Therefore in this phrase, if one keeps before him a clear perception of the figure, at one time the idea of fabricating, at another that of ploughing, is presented before us. The usage of the language in the case before us is more in favour of the latter than of the former. Whether ישׁב את means to dwell together with, or as Böttcher, to sit together with, after <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>; Psa 26:4., need not be a matter of dispute. It means in general a continued being together, whether as sitting, <reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job 2:13</reference>, or as dwelling, Jdg 17:11.<note placement="foot">Accentuate והוא־יושׁב לבטח. It is thus in correct texts. The <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> is transformed, according to the <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xviii. §2.</note> <div eID="gen10644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10645" type="x-p"/> To take advantage of the regardlessness of him who imparts to us his confidence is unamiable. Love is doubly owing to him who resigns himself to it because he believes in it.
entries.6a8eef074f3b73d6cb07a36e163af4def3c0b7ad: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.30">Pro 3:30</reference> <div eID="gen10645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10646" type="x-p"/> A third illustration of the same principle is peaceableness: <div eID="gen10646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10647" type="x-p"/> Contend not with a man without a cause, <div eID="gen10647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10648" type="x-p"/> When he has inflicted no evil upon thee. <div eID="gen10648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10649" type="x-p"/> Instead of תּרוּב, or as the Kerı̂ has amended it תּריב, the abbreviated form תּרב or תּרב would be more correct after אל; רוּב or ריב (from רב, to be compact) means to fall upon one another, to come to hand-blows, to contend. Contending and quarrelling with a man, whoever he may be, without sufficient reason, ought to be abandoned; but there exists no such reason if he has done me no harm which I have to reproach him with. גּמל רעה with the accus. or dat. of the person signifies to bring evil upon any one, <hi type="italic">malum inferre</hi>, or also <hi type="italic">referre</hi> (Schultens), for גּמל (cogn. גּמר) signifies to execute, to complete, accomplish - both of the initiative and of the requital, both of the anticipative and of the recompensing action; here in the former of these senses.
entries.72ca612e1fdd58969e05c27b80c374aa49fadc1f: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.31-Prov.3.32">Pro 3:31-32</reference> <div eID="gen10649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10650" type="x-p"/> These exhortations to neighbourly love in the form of warning against whatever is opposed to it, are followed by the warning against fellowship with the loveless: 31 Be not envious toward the man of violence,      And have no pleasure in all his ways. 32 For an abhorrence to Jahve is the perverse,      But with the upight is His secret. <div eID="gen10650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10651" type="x-p"/> The conceptions of jealousy and envy lie in קנּא (derived by Schultens from קנא, Arab. ḳanâ, <hi type="italic">intensius rubere</hi>) inseparable from each other. The lxx, which for תקנא reads תקנה (κτήσῃ), brings the envy into 31b, as if the words here were ואל־תּתחר, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1">Psa 37:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference> (there the lxx has μὴ παραζήλου, here μηδὲ ζηλώσῃς). There is no reason for correcting our text in accordance with this (substituting תּתחר for תּבחר as Hitzig does), because בּכל־דּרכיו would be too vague an expression for the object of the envy, while אל־תבחר altogether agrees with it; and the contrary remark, that בּחר בּכּל is fundamentally no בחר, fails since (1) בחר frequently expresses pleasure in anything without the idea of choice, and (2) “have not pleasure in all his ways” is in the Hebrew style equivalent to “in any one of his ways;” Ewald, §323b. He who does “violence to the law” (Zep 3:4) becomes thereby, according to the common course of the world, a person who is feared, whose authority, power, and resources are increased, but one must not therefore envy him, nor on any side take pleasure in his conduct, which in all respects is to be reprobated; for the נלוז, <hi type="italic">inflexus, tortuosus</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>), who swerves from the right way and goes in a crooked false way, is an object of Jahve’s abhorrence, while, on the contrary, the just, who with a right mind walks in the right way, is Jahve’s סוד - an echo of Psa 25:14. סוד (R. סד, to be firm, compressed) means properly the being pressed together, or sitting together (cf. the Arab. wisâd, wisâdt, a cushion, divan, corresponding in form to the Hebr. יסוד) for the purpose of private communication and conversation (הוּסד), and then partly the confidential intercourse, as here (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.29.4">Job 29:4</reference>), partly the private communication, the secret (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Amo 3:7</reference>). lxx, ἐν δὲ δικαίοις [οὐ] συνεδριάζει. Those who are out of the way, who prefer to the simplicity of right-doing all manner of crooked ways, are contrary to God, and He may have nothing to do with them; but the right-minded He makes partakers of His most intimate intercourse, He deals with them as His friends.
entries.0b12fd6949dcff215af33c9d21fdac285829f318: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.33">Pro 3:33</reference> <div eID="gen10651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10652" type="x-p"/> The prosperity of the godless, far from being worthy of envy, has as its reverse side the curse: <div eID="gen10652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10653" type="x-p"/> The curse of Jahve is in the house of the godless, <div eID="gen10653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10654" type="x-p"/> And the dwelling of the just He blesseth. מארה (a curse), like מסלּה (a highway, from סלל), is formed from ארר (cf. Arab. harr, <hi type="italic">detestari, abhorrere</hi>, a word-imitation of an interjection used in disagreeable experiences). The curse is not merely a deprivation of external goods which render life happy, and the blessing is not merely the fulness of external possessions; the central-point of the curse lies in continuous disquiet of conscience, and that of the blessing in the happy consciousness that God is with us, in soul-rest and peace which is certain of the grace and goodness of God. The poetic נוה (from נוה = Arab. nwy, <hi type="italic">tetendit aliquo</hi>) signifies the place of settlement, and may be a word borrowed from a nomad life, since it denotes specially the pasture-ground; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.15">Pro 24:15</reference> (Fleischer). While the curse of God rests in the house of the wicked (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Köhler on Zec 5:4), He blesses, on the contrary, the dwelling-place of the righteous. The lxx and Jerome read יברך, but יברך is more agreeable, since God continues to be the subject.
entries.a8d9aaff537f3a13dd18a825077cd6f17eaa0382: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.34">Pro 3:34</reference> <div eID="gen10654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10655" type="x-p"/> His relation to men is determined by their relation to Him. <div eID="gen10655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10656" type="x-p"/> As for the scorners, He scorneth them, <div eID="gen10656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10657" type="x-p"/> But to the lowly He giveth grace. <div eID="gen10657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10658" type="x-p"/> Most interpreters render the verse thus: “If the scorner He (even He, in return) scorneth, so He (on the other hand) giveth grace to the lowly.” For the sequence of the words in the consequence, in which the precedence of the verb is usual, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.12.5">Lev 12:5</reference>, we are referred to <reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">Pro 23:18</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.14">Pro 24:14</reference>; but why had the poet placed the two facts in the relation of condition and consequence? The one fact is not the consequence but the reverse of the other, and accordingly they are opposed to each other in coordinated passages, Psa 18:26. The <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> in such antitheses has generally the meaning of “and on the other hand,” <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.20">Job 8:20</reference>, while the lxx, Targ., Syriac, and Jerome altogether pass over the אם as if it did not exist. Ziegler translates: “Truly! the scorner He scorneth;” but an affirmative אם does not exist, the asseveration after the manner of an oath is negative. Bertheau’s expedient would be more acceptable, by which he makes the whole of <reference osisRef="Prov.3.34">Pro 3:34</reference> the protasis to <reference osisRef="Prov.3.35">Pro 3:35</reference>; but if this were intended, another subject would not enter into Pro 3:35. Thus 34a and 34b are two independent parallel passages; אם־ללּצים is the protasis: if as regards the scorners, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, if His conduct is directed to the scorners, so He scorneth. The ל denotes relation, and in this elliptical usage is like the ל of superscription, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Jer 23:9. הוּא is the emphatic αὐτός: He on the contrary, and in a decisive way (Ewald, §314ab). Instead of יליץ fo  there might have been used יליצם (for הליץ, where it occurs as a governing word, has the accusative, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.28">Pro 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.51">Psa 119:51</reference>), but we do not miss the object: if it relates to scorners (thus also Löwenstein translates), so it is He in return who scorneth. The lxx renders it: κύριος ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν; cf. Jam 4:6; 1Pe 5:5. הוּא is used as a name of God (<hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitschr.</hi> xvi. 400), on which account it is rendered like יהוה by κύριος. A ὑπερήφανος (appearing above others, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, overbearing) is the לץ, according to the definition Pro 21:24. the expression of the <hi type="italic">talio</hi> is generalized in ἀντιτάσσεται (resists them). For עניים the Kerı̂ has ענוים: ענו (from ענה, the ground-form ענו, Arab. 'anaw) is the lowly (ταπεινός), or he who bends himself, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the gentle and humble, the patient, and the passive עני, he who is bowed down, the suffering; but the limits of the conception are moveable, since in עני is presupposed the possession of fruit-virtues gained in the school of affliction.
entries.055b7a7e7abc8a71b187803cab1d5c2360ce04d5: <reference osisRef="Prov.3.35">Pro 3:35</reference> <div eID="gen10658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10659" type="x-p"/> This group of the proverbs of wisdom now suitably closes with the fundamental contrast between the wise and fools: <div eID="gen10659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10660" type="x-p"/> The wise shall inherit honour, <div eID="gen10660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10661" type="x-p"/> But fools carry away shame. <div eID="gen10661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10662" type="x-p"/> If we take וּכסילים as the object, then we can scarcely interpret the clause: shame sweeps fools away (Umbreit, Zöckler, Bertheau), for הרים [<hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of רוּם] signifies (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.14">Isa 57:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.31">Eze 21:31</reference>) “to raise up anything high and far,” not “to sweep away.” Preferable is the rendering: τοὺς δ ̓ ἄφρονας ὑψοῖ ἀτιμία (<hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi>, and similarly Jerome), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, only to it do they owe their celebrity as warning examples (Ewald), to which Oetinger compares “whose glory is in their shame,” <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Phi 3:19</reference>;<note placement="foot">Jona Gerundi renders it otherwise: “But shame raises the fools high;” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, only the infamous, he who has no sense of honour, makes much advancement out of fools.</note> but קלון is the contrary of כּבוד (glory, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.16">Hab 2:16</reference>), and therefore is as much an object conception as is the latter, 35a. If it is the object, then if we take מרים from מר after the form of לן, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.21">Neh 13:21</reference> = ממירים (Hos 4:7), it might be rendered: Yet fools exchange shame (Löwenstein). But מוּר, like the Arab. mrr, <hi type="italic">transire</hi>, means properly to pass over or to wander over; it is intransitive, and only in <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. signifies actively to exchange. מרים thus will be the participle of הרים; the plur. taken distributively (fools = whoever is only always a fool) is connected with the singular of the predicate. This change in the number is here, however, more difficult than at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pro 3:18</reference>, and in other places, where the plur. of the part. permits the resolution into a relative clause with <hi type="italic">quicunque</hi>, and more difficult than at <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Pro 28:1</reference>, where the sing. of the predicate is introduced by attraction; wherefore מרים may be an error in transcribing for מרימים or מרימי (Böttcher). J. H. Michaelis (after the Targ. and Syr.) has properly rendered the clause: “<hi type="italic">stulti tollunt ignominiam tanquam portionem suam</hi>,” adding “<hi type="italic">quae derivato nomine </hi>תרומה<hi type="italic">dicitur</hi>.” הרים signifies, in the language of the sacrificial worship and of worship generally, to lift off from anything the best portion, the legitimate portion due to God and the priesthood (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.9">Pro 3:9</reference>); for which reason Rashi glosses מרים by מפרישׁ לו, and Ralbag by מגביה לו. See Pro 14:29. Honour is that which the wise inherit, it falls to them unsought as a possession, but fools receive shame as the offal (viz., of their foolish conduct). The fut. and part. are significantly interchanged. The life of the wise ends in glory, but fools inherit shame; the fruit of their conduct is shame and evermore shame.  <chapter eID="Prov.3"/> <div eID="gen10662" type="x-p"/>

Having commanded doing of good, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27, 28. he here forbids doing or designing any evil.</ns0:note> against thy neighbor, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Relying upon thine integrity: do not therefore betray thy trust, which is hateful even to Heathens.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30. Strive not <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Either by words before the Magistrate; or otherwise by thine actions.</ns0:note> with a man without cause <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Without just and necessary cause.</ns0:note>, if he have done thee no harm <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Whereby he clearly implies, that in case of injury a Man may by all lawful means defend himself.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 37. 1.</ns0:note> Envy thou not <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a man of violence.</ns0:note> the oppressor <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">For his impunity and success in his wicked designs, and the Wealth which he gains by his unrighteous practices.</ns0:note>, and choose none of his ways <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For what men envy in others they seek to obtain for themselves.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32. For the froward <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>perverse,</ns0:hi> who walketh in crooked or sinful paths as the Oppressour last mentioned; opposed to the upright Man, who is called <ns0:hi>right</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>straight,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 4. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 29. 27.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> abomination to the LORD <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">God hates him and therefore sooner or later he must needs be extremely and eternally miserable.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 25. 14.</ns0:note> but his secret <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with the righteous <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">They are God's Friends and Favourites, to whom he familiarly imparts, as men use to do to their Friends, his mind and counsels, or his secret favours and comforts to which other men are strangers. Compare <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 25. 14. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 15. 15. <ns0:hi>Revel.</ns0:hi> 2. 17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Levit. 26. 14, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Mal. 2. 2.</ns0:note> The Curse of the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the house of the wicked <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Not onely upon his own Person, but also upon his Posterity and upon all his domestical concerns.</ns0:note>: but he blesseth the habitation of the just.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jam. 4. 6. 1 Pet. 5. 5.</ns0:note> Surely he scorneth <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He will expose them to scorn and contempt.</ns0:note> the scorners <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Proud and insolent Sinners, who <ns0:hi>make a mock at sin,</ns0:hi> Prov. 14. 9. and at God and Religion also, and despise all counsels and means of amendment. Comp. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 1. 1. & <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1. 22.</ns0:note>: but he giveth grace <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To wit, favour, both with himself and with men, as this Word and Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 3. 21. & 11. 3. & 12. 36. <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 9. 11. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2. 52. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> unto the lowly.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35. The wise shall inherit glory <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Shall enjoy it not onely for a season, as wicked men oft-times do, but as an Inheritance constantly and to perpetuity.</ns0:note>, but shame <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> exalteth the fools.</ns0:note> shall be the promotion of fools <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In stead of that glory which they greedily seek they shall meet with nothing but ignominy. Or, as it is in the Margent, <ns0:hi>shame exalteth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>lifteth up fools, i. e.</ns0:hi> it makes them manifest and notorious, as this very word is used, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 14. 29. Or, as the words lie in the He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew Text, <ns0:hi>fools take</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>carry away</ns0:hi> (as this word is here rendred by divers both ancient and modern Translators, and as it is used, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 6. 10. 15. and oft elsewhere) <ns0:hi>shame,</ns0:hi> to wit, as his proper Portion or Inheritance; which is here very fitly opposed to the Portion or Inheritance of the Just. And although the Verb be singular, yet it agrees well enough with the Noun plural, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause this is taken distributively, such constructions being very usual in the Hebrew Text.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
